meta.title: Tessellum · Measure behaviour, not just opinions
meta.description: A free, bilingual research instrument with three modules: a 3D shopping village, an e-commerce simulator and forms, on one calibrated engine.

hero.body: Five research tools on one platform: a 3D shopping village, an e-commerce simulator, forms, social network analysis and sentiment analysis. Each works on its own; combine them when a study needs it.
hero.figureLabel: A cube of light points that turns with the pointer. Three points glow brighter: the variables under study.

modules.title: Five tools. Each works on its own; combine them when a study needs it.

village.name: Shopping village
village.body: A realistic 3D street, mall, souq or supermarket aisle. Participants walk between stores, look at windows and ads, go in and buy.
village.records: Approaches, store entries, dwell time, ads seen, purchases.

shop.name: E-commerce simulator
shop.body: A realistic online shop: search, filters, product pages, sponsored placements and a simulated checkout, with the same products and offers.
shop.records: Searches, clicks, product views, basket changes, checkout.

forms.name: Forms
forms.body: Questionnaires and consent with thirteen question types, image and video stimuli, and choice and judgement tasks.

network.name: Social network analysis
network.kind: Analyse who is connected to whom
network.body: Upload an edge list and explore the network: the most central accounts, the communities, and how tightly it holds together.
network.records: Nothing is collected. You upload your own file, and it is analysed on your device.

sentiment.name: Sentiment analysis
sentiment.body: Upload texts you have already labelled positive, negative or neutral, and compare the distribution across accounts, categories or languages.
sentiment.records: Nothing is collected. The labels are yours; the tool counts and compares them.

environments.title: Eleven places. One experiment.
environments.body: In the shopping village the researcher chooses where the study happens. The place changes; the stores, offers, products and recorded events stay exactly the same, so results compare across scenes.
environments.avatar: Each participant's figure is assigned automatically from their own answers. Anyone who prefers not to say walks as a circle of light, with no body or gender given.

engine.title: Between, within and mixed designs, assigned on the server.
engine.body: Balanced conditions with quotas. Factors mapped by random draw, full permutation or Latin square. Every assigned value is saved with the session and the locked study version.
engine.caption: target_brand · Latin square (3) · which brand shows its AI-generated ad
engine.note: The square marker repeats the colour, so the pattern reads without colour too.

data.title: Four files. Nothing to clean.
data.body: A participant-level CSV, the event log, a bilingual codebook and SPSS syntax, with Arabic intact and the study configuration attached.

bilingual.here: Designed in two directions at once: left to right, and right to left.
bilingual.other: مصمّمة في الاتجاهين معًا: من اليمين إلى اليسار، ومن اليسار إلى اليمين.

footer.status: Tessellum is in development. The shopping village, e-commerce simulator and forms are working prototypes; the two analysis tools are being built.

network.name: Social network analysis
network.summary: See how accounts are connected: who is central, which communities form, and how dense the network is.
network.need1: A CSV or Excel file with one row per connection (an edge list): a source column and a target column. A weight column is optional. Exports from 4CAT and Communalytic, and Gephi's GEXF and GraphML files, are read directly.
network.need2: Optional: a second file describing each account (type, followers, category), used to colour the network.
network.need3: Whether connections have a direction (A mentions B) or not (A and B are linked).
network.get1: For each account: degree, betweenness, closeness and PageRank.
network.get2: For the whole network: density, clustering, number of connected components and diameter.
network.get3: Communities found with the Louvain method, coloured automatically.
network.get4: An interactive network you can drag, zoom and filter, with PNG, SVG and CSV exports.
network.get5: A short report that explains the numbers in plain language, with the method, the settings and the usual cautions, ready for a methods chapter.
network.limit1: Networks up to about 50,000 accounts are shown interactively. For very large networks some measures are estimated, and the results say so.
network.limit2: If your file has a sentiment column, accounts can be coloured by sentiment.
network.need4: No edge list? Upload a table of posts (author, text, date) and the tool builds the network from mentions, replies and shared hashtags.

sentiment.name: Sentiment analysis
sentiment.summary: Summarise and compare sentiment labels you have already assigned to your texts.
sentiment.need1: A CSV file with a text column and a label column: positive, negative or neutral, or a number from -1 to 1.
sentiment.need2: Optional columns: account, category, language, dialect or country, and date, used for comparisons.
sentiment.get1: The distribution of positive, negative and neutral texts.
sentiment.get2: Average sentiment for each account or category, with the number of texts behind each average.
sentiment.get3: Comparisons between groups, and between languages if the file has a language column.
sentiment.get4: Charts and tables you can export.
sentiment.limit1: This version does not classify texts automatically. It counts and compares the labels in your file.
sentiment.limit2: Automatic classification for English and Gulf Arabic is planned for a later version, with stated accuracy for each language.
sentiment.disclaimer: The labels are the researcher's responsibility. This tool only aggregates and displays them.
sentiment.need3: Optional: a second coder's label column, to measure how far the coders agree.
sentiment.get5: Agreement between coders (Krippendorff's alpha), with a plain reading of the score.
sentiment.get6: A list of the texts the coders disagreed on, to settle one by one and export a final label.

privacy.title: Protecting the people in your data
privacy.intro: Before you upload a file, remove anything that identifies a real person unless your ethics approval allows it.
privacy.p1: Use codes such as A001 and A002 in place of usernames, and keep the list that links codes to names in a separate, protected file. A built-in anonymising button is coming with the upload step.
privacy.p2Title: Remove what you do not need
privacy.p2: Delete columns the analysis does not use, such as profile links, email addresses, phone numbers and locations.
privacy.p3: A quoted post can be searched for and traced back to its author. Paraphrase quotations in publications where anonymity matters.
privacy.p4Title: What happens to your file here
privacy.p4: Your file is analysed on your own device. It is not sent to a server, and it is not kept after you close the page unless you choose to save it.
privacy.p5Title: What this platform does not do
privacy.p5: It does not collect data from social media platforms. You are responsible for how your data was obtained and for following the platform's terms and your institution's ethics rules.

results.noFileBody: Uploaded files are kept only while the page is open, so a reload clears them. Upload your file again to see the results.
results.leftOutDetail: {blank} without a label, {unread} with a label that was not recognised
results.noGroups: The file has no account, category, language or dialect column matched, so there are no groups to compare. Match one on the upload step.
results.smallNote: Groups with fewer than {n} texts are shown but left out of the test: their figures can change a lot with one or two texts.
results.missing: {n, plural, one {# text has} other {# texts have}} no value in this column and {n, plural, one {is} other {are}} not shown.
results.more: Showing the {shown} largest of {total} groups. The export has all of them.
results.testTitle: Is the difference more than chance?
results.testNone: A test needs at least two groups with {n} or more texts each.
results.testYes: The groups differ in their mix of positive, neutral and negative texts by more than chance would explain.
results.testNo: The differences between the groups are within what chance alone could produce.
results.testDetail: Chi-square = {chi2}, df = {df}, p {p}, Cramér's V = {v} ({strength}), across {groups} groups and {n} texts.
results.testLow: This comparison cannot be tested reliably: {pct}% of the expected counts are below 5. Merge small categories or collect more texts before drawing a conclusion.
results.testReminder: A significant difference says the groups differ, not why. The labels are the researcher's own.
results.trendUnread: {n, plural, one {# date was} other {# dates were}} not read. Use the year-first form, for example 2026-03-14, because 03/04/2026 means different days in different countries.
results.trendOne: All dated texts fall in one period, so there is no trend to draw.
results.method1: Only rows with a recognised label are counted. The tool does not classify any text.
results.method2Cat: Net sentiment is the share of positive texts minus the share of negative texts: each positive text counts 1, each neutral 0, each negative -1, and the result is the average.
results.method2Num: Every label in this file is a number from -1 to 1, so net sentiment is the average of those numbers. A text counts as positive above 0.05, negative below -0.05, and neutral in between.
results.method3: Groups are compared with a chi-square test of independence on the counts of positive, neutral and negative texts. Cramér's V shows how strong the association is: under 0.1 weak, 0.1 to 0.3 moderate, above 0.3 strong.
results.trendSmall: Most periods have fewer than {n} texts, so the line moves a lot from one text to the next. Read the overall direction, not single points.

review.agreementHint: Two label columns were matched. Alpha corrects for agreement expected by chance: 1 is perfect agreement, 0 is chance, below 0 is worse than chance.
review.agreementNone: Alpha cannot be computed: the coders used only one category, or there are too few texts.

alphaReading.fair: below the usual 0.667 threshold; resolve the disagreements before reporting

review.disagreeHint: Choose the final label for each text. Choices change the results and the export. Texts left undecided keep the first coder's label.
review.disagreeCount: {n, plural, one {# text disagreed} other {# texts disagreed}}
review.moreRows: Showing the first {shown} of {total}. The export includes all of them.
review.exportHint: Every file is UTF-8 with a byte order mark, so Excel shows Arabic correctly. Column names are in English so they match the analysis software.
review.exportNote: The data file includes the text. Anonymise accounts on the upload step first if your ethics approval requires it.
noteMethod: Only labels the researcher supplied are counted. The tool does not classify text.
Net sentiment is the share of positive texts minus negative texts, from -1 to +1; numeric labels are averaged as given.
Groups are compared with a chi-square test of independence on counts of positive, neutral and negative texts; Cramér's V gives the strength of association.
review.noteNone: No second coder was used, so agreement was not measured.
noteCautions: The labels are the researcher's responsibility; the tool only counts and compares them.
Small groups give unstable figures; check the group sizes before reading differences.
A significant difference shows the groups differ, not why.
review.pickFinal: Choose the final label for text {n}
review.noDataAction: Upload a file first. Uploaded files are kept only while the page is open.
